cells.tense: The practice is being kept, and attention is doing the keeping rather than force.
cells.ask: Show one person the ordinary version of your practice this week — the rough take, the unfinished pass — before you refine it any further.
cells.core:
You keep a practice going, and the striking thing is how little force is in it. Attention holds it up. Not flash, not a big push — the same small hour, kept. Time alone with it isn't hiding from anyone; it's simply where the work happens. Things get sharper because you kept showing up, not because you worried them into shape.

That steadiness is free to feed something next. When a structure in your life falls away — a plan, a way of working, something you held to — you don't have to rebuild it out of fear. You can clear out the part that was false and keep going. So leave the practice a little unfinished this week. Show the rough draft, not the polished one, and give someone's response room to matter. The balance holds because you keep it lit. It costs you the comfort of only showing what's done.
cells.sheetLine: You keep a small practice lit, and you keep it that way on purpose.
cells.verb: keeping a small steady practice lit by attention alone
cells.place: in the private hours where repetition turns intention into skill

cells.tense: You keep refining ahead of a version of yourself that hasn't shown up yet, and the refining is outrunning the work itself.
cells.ask: Stop one session at good enough instead of finished, and leave it alone for a full day before you touch it again.
cells.core:
Somewhere ahead is the day it finally comes out right, and you're already living in it. So each session becomes a test. Refining used to be part of the work; now it's the whole point. You fix, you compare, you fix again, and under it is the fear of what happens if you ever stop. Being alone with it starts to feel required rather than chosen. That's the tell — the practice used to connect you to something, and now it's a room you don't leave.

There's another way to stop, and it isn't pushing harder. It's finishing. When something is done, you let it go, even if it isn't perfect. So run one session to good enough and then walk away from it for a day. Leave the tool where it sits. Nothing is lost that way, and the practice gets to be a practice again instead of a verdict. What it costs is the grip.
cells.sheetLine: You're refining toward a moment that hasn't arrived, and the grip has become the practice.
cells.verb: keeping a small steady practice lit by attention alone
cells.place: in the private hours where repetition turns intention into skill

cells.tense: A door closed behind you at some point, and you're still standing on the near side of it.
cells.ask: Pick up one practice for ten minutes today, any one, and stop on purpose — then note what setting it down was like, not how well it went.
cells.core:
You know what a kept practice looks like from the outside, and you don't have one right now. Not because you don't care. Keeping it started to feel like a risk, and the part of you that used to reach for it went quiet. The ability to sustain and refine is still in you. It just doesn't have anywhere to stand. What's missing is a fair sense of what you get for showing up, and what you're allowed to keep from it.

So don't force a practice back. Start smaller than that. Pick up one thing for ten minutes, set it down on purpose, and notice what setting it down was like. The point isn't the ten minutes — it's getting a clear read on what the practice is worth to you before it asks for anything. If a session goes badly, that says something about the session, not about you. Nothing after it depends on it having gone well.
cells.sheetLine: The practice isn't gone. What went missing is a fair sense of what it's worth to keep.
cells.verb: keeping a small steady practice lit by attention alone
cells.place: in the private hours where repetition turns intention into skill

cells.tense: You're already good at something from hours nobody counted, and you keep calling it a thing you just happen to be able to do.
cells.ask: Think of one skill people come to you for, and tell one of them where it came from — even just that you put time into it.
cells.core:
There's a skill in your hands that people come to you for, and when they ask how you got it, the answer comes out as a shrug. You didn't count the hours. They were yours, in your own time, and they turned into something real. That's a practice. It's running right now, filed under just being able to do it, and the person it actually belongs to hasn't said so out loud.

You don't need to work out what it all means before you open your mouth. You can move through not knowing without forcing it shut — you don't need the whole road mapped, just enough light to name one thing. So think of one skill and tell one person where it came from. Even partway is enough. What it costs is the story where it arrived by itself.
cells.sheetLine: The skill in your hands came from hours you kept, and you've been calling it luck.
cells.verb: keeping a small steady practice lit by attention alone
cells.place: in the private hours where repetition turns intention into skill
